To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the political polarization of the general public is higher when discussing ”fake news” compared to other political topics and (ii) users tend to report as ”fake news” information that is related to political topics that they disagree with.
”Fake news” related tweets are more polarized in terms of the associated political leaning than non-”fake news” related tweets.

1) the political polarization of users is higher when they are talking about ”fake news” than when they are not, and 2) the political polarization between users who share ”fake news” and those who share other information is higher than between users who do not talk about ”fake news”.

the relationship between political polariza­tion and the spread of misinformation, and how polarization may be a factor responsible for the creation of distinct narratives on what constitutes misinformation.
understanding whether political polarization is a factor in the spread and perception of ”fake news”.
how polarization may affect the spread of misinformation, and how this may impact the design of misinformation detection systems.

the polarization of the users is increasing, and this polarization is related to the spread of ”fake news”.

there is a strong correlation between the political polarization of a user, and the likelihood that they label information that they disagree with as ”fake news”.

the polarization between the political parties in the US has increased in recent years, and that this polarization has been reflected on what users consider as ”fake news” and what they do not.
